'''''Heuchera''''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|h|juː|k|ᵻ|r|ə}} {{respell|HEW|kih|rə}}<ref>''Sunset Western Garden Book.'' 1995. 606–607.</ref> or {{IPAc-en|ˈ|h|ɔɪ||k|ə|r|ə}} {{respell|HOY|kih|rə}}<ref>"heuchera, n.". OED Online. June 2021. Oxford University Press.  https://www.oed.com/view/Entry/86545?redirectedFrom=Heuchera  (accessed June 16, 2021).</ref>) is a genus of largely evergreen<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.plantsforshade.co.uk/acatalog/Heuchera.html |title=Heuchera |access-date=2016-06-11 |archive-date=2019-02-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190209063601/http://plantsforshade.co.uk/acatalog/Heuchera.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> [[perennial plant]]s in the family [[Saxifragaceae]]. All species are native to [[North America]] except for ''[[Heuchera sichotensis]]'', native to the [[Russian Far East]].<ref>[https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:3271093-4 ''Heuchera sichotensis'' (Gorovoj & N.S.Pavlova) Zhmylev]. ''[[Plants of the World Online]]''. Retrieved 13 April 2024.</ref> Common names include '''alumroot''' and '''coral bells'''.<ref>{{cite web |first=Nikki |last=Phipps |title=Planting Coral Bells: Tips For Growing The Coral Bells Plant In Your Garden |date=October 2011 |url=http://www.gardeningknowhow.com/ornamental/flowers/coral-bells/coral-bells-plant.htm |publisher=gardeningknowhow.com |access-date=21 December 2016}}</ref>

==Description==
''Heuchera'' have [[palmate]]ly lobed leaves on long [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]]s, and a thick, woody [[rootstock]]. The genus was named after [[Johann Heinrich von Heucher]] (1677–1746), an 18th-century [[Germany|German]] physician,<ref name="fna">[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=115382 ''Heuchera''.] Flora of North America.</ref> and Professor at [[University of Halle-Wittenberg|Wittenberg University]].<ref>Archibald William Smith {{Google books|ahNMkgoNJ7IC|A Gardener's Handbook of Plant Names: Their Meanings and Origins |page=185}}</ref> There are approximately 37 species, but the [[taxonomy (biology)|taxonomy]] of the genus is difficult because the species often intergrade with one another, [[hybrid (biology)|hybridization]] is common, and the flowers change markedly in proportion as they develop.<ref name="fna" />

==Distribution and habitat==
Alumroot species grow in varied habitats, so some species look quite different from one another, and have varying preferences regarding temperature, soil, and other natural factors. ''H. maxima'' is found on the [[Channel Islands of California]], where it grows on rocky, windy, saline-washed ocean shores, and ''H. sanguinea'', called '''coral bells''' because of its [[cerise (color)|cerise]] [[flower]]s, can be found in the warm, dry canyons of [[Mexico]] and adjacent [[New Mexico]] and [[Arizona]].  In the Mid-Atlantic region of the United States, the plants grow best in shade.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://mtcubacenter.org/trials/heuchera/|title=Heuchera for the Mid-Atlantic Region|last=Coombs|first=George|date=2014|website=Mt. Cuba Center|access-date=27 January 2017}}</ref>

Several alumroots and their crosses are used as [[ornamental plant]]s.<ref name=fna/>

==Uses==
[[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Native American peoples]] used some ''Heuchera'' species medicinally. The [[Tlingit people|Tlingit]] used ''H. glabra'' as an herbal remedy for inflammation of the [[testicle]]s caused by [[syphilis]].<ref name=glabra>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=250065935 ''Heuchera glabra''.] Flora of North America.</ref> To the [[Navajo people|Navajo]], ''H. novamexicana'' was a [[Panacea (medicine)|panacea]] and a pain reliever.<ref name=fna-nova>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=250065970 '' Heuchera novamexicana''.] Flora of North America.</ref> The roots of ''H. cylindrica'' had a variety of medicinal uses among the [[Blackfoot Confederacy|Blackfoot]], [[Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes of the Flathead Nation|Flathead]], [[Ktunaxa|Kutenai]], [[Okanagan people|Okanagan]], [[Colville (tribe)|Colville]], and [[Secwepemc|Shuswap]].<ref name=fna-cyl>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=250065967 ''Heuchera cylindrica''.] Flora of North America.</ref>

==Cultivation==
The majority of ''Heuchera'' sold for gardens are hybrids of ''[[Heuchera americana|H. americana]]'', such as 'Green Spice'.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZyRkV3matEoC |title=Armitage's Garden Perennials |via=[[Google Books]]|isbn=9780881924350 |access-date=2013-04-01|last1=Armitage |first1=Allan M. |year=2000 |publisher=Timber Press }}</ref>
The original 'Purple Palace' discovered in a [[palace]] in England is believed to be a ''H. micrantha'' × ''H. villosa'' hybrid,<ref name=cull>Cullina, W. [https://books.google.com/books?id=aLlt53wiYr8C ''New England Wild Flower Society Guide to Growing and Propagating Wildflowers of the United States and Canada''.] Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2000. {{ISBN|0-395-96609-4}}, {{ISBN|978-0-395-96609-9}}</ref> which was then crossed with ''H. americana''. Another group of hybrids are crosses of ''Heuchera'' with ''[[Tiarella]]'' treated under the name [[× Heucherella|× ''Heucherella'']]. Gardeners and horticulturists have developed a multitude of hybrids between various ''Heuchera'' species. There is an extensive array of blossom sizes, shapes, and colors, foliage types, and geographic tolerances. They are valued as foliage plants, producing rosettes of leaves in shades of green, pink and bronze, often [[variegation|variegated]] or textured; with long [[thyrse]]s of white, green, pink or red flowers in spring.
